messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 70
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Photographer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 75

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Meaning Seeking: I think about why the event has happened to me, Face Hiding: cover face with hands, Emotion Control: I try hard to control my emotions
  Memory: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame, Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
  Negative Appraisals: No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Maya had spent seventy years trying to outrun a memory that would not stay buried. When she finally sat down in the consulting room, her hands were folded in her lap, palms pressed flat against her thighs as if to keep them from rising on their own. She was a photographer by trade, a woman whose life had been built around framing and controlling what the world saw, and yet here she was, unable to look the therapist in the eye for more than a few seconds at a time.

The abuse had happened when she was a child, in the small apartment her family shared with her maternal uncle. She did not remember the first time he hit her, or the last. She could not deliberately recall most of it at all — when she tried, the details slipped away like water through fingers, leaving only a thick fog of dread and the sensation of her own small body bracing for impact. What she remembered instead was shame. A shame so complete and so physical that it lived in her bones. When a stray sound or a certain quality of afternoon light brushed against the edges of that buried memory, the shame would surge up without warning, hot and suffocating, and she would find herself pressing both hands to her face, fingers spread wide, hiding from nothing and everything at once.

The terror was just as immediate. Remembering, even fleetingly, brought back the same raw fear she had felt as a girl — the certainty that she was about to be destroyed, that no one would come, that she was utterly alone in a world that did not care. She had learned early to control her emotions with an iron will. She became expert at smoothing her face into neutrality, at swallowing her voice before it could tremble, at making herself small and still. But the effort was exhausting, and it never truly worked. The emotions simply waited, coiled beneath the surface, ready to spring.

As an adult, Maya had built a life around the belief that she could not afford to be vulnerable. She divorced her husband after fifteen years, partly because she could not explain to him why she sometimes froze in the hallway when he raised his voice, even if he was only calling her to dinner. She had come to believe that she no longer belonged anywhere — not in her family, not in her community, not even in her own body. The people who had hurt her faced no consequences. Her uncle had lived out his life respected and unbothered, while Maya carried the weight of what he had done in every cell of her being. That injustice had calcified into a quiet, bitter certainty: the world did not protect people like her. She had to be on guard all the time.

Her work as a photographer kept her moving, which suited her. She took portraits for a living, but she had developed an elaborate way of working that kept her subjects at a distance — she shot from behind the camera, she rarely spoke during sessions, and she avoided any assignment that required her to be in close quarters with men of a certain age and build. The trigger was specific but unpredictable: a particular tone of voice, a hand raised to adjust a collar, the shadow of a tall figure blocking a doorway. When it happened, she would feel the shame rise and her hands would fly to her face, and she would have to excuse herself to the bathroom, where she would stand trembling and furious at herself for still being afraid.

The consequences had accumulated quietly over decades. Her social world had shrunk to almost nothing. She had few friends and no close confidants. She turned down invitations to family gatherings because the thought of sitting in a room full of people who might ask about her life felt unbearable. She had come to see herself as fundamentally separate from others — a person who had been broken in a way that could not be repaired and could not be explained.

What finally brought Maya to seek help was not the shame or the terror or the hypervigilance, though all of those were as present as ever. It was a moment in her studio, three weeks before the intake, when she was photographing a young mother and her infant daughter. The mother had laughed, a warm and easy sound, and the baby had reached up to touch her face. Maya had felt something crack open inside her chest — a longing so vast and so painful that she had nearly dropped her camera. She had gone home that evening and sat in the dark for hours, and for the first time in her life, she had allowed herself to think: I cannot keep living like this. She was not sure what she hoped for in therapy. She was not even sure she believed it could help. But she was terrified of what would happen if she did not try.
